Now let’s talk about how to coordinate with contractors. This coordination mainly occurs during the construction phase. In North America, for example, the design institute is responsible for chairing construction meetings, which are held every two weeks or weekly.

Another task is preparing meeting minutes, followed by reviewing shop drawings. When our team in Egypt worked on the new capital project, we prepared numerous shop drawings. The design institute often rejected them multiple times because the specifications outline the submission requirements for shop drawings or close-out documents. If the requirements aren’t met, the design institute has the right to reject them, as the specifications are what the contractor committed to during the bidding process.

If the specifications do not impose additional requirements for shop drawings, the contractor may push back and request extra fees, arguing that the work falls outside the original scope.

A site instruction is an on-site notice issued by the engineer, which may involve modifications, cancellations, additions, or changes. Triggers for site instructions include the engineer identifying an issue, the contractor raising a question, or the client requesting a change.

There is also the CCM (Contemplated Change Notice), typically triggered by a site instruction. If a site instruction results in an increase, decrease, or alteration to the contractor’s scope of work, the design institute issues a CCM, equivalent to a domestic change order. It details the reasons and content of the change and requests the contractor to provide a quote.

After receiving the CCM, the contractor prepares a quote for the client, who then forwards it to the design institute for review to assess whether the quote is reasonable. Once approved, it becomes a change order. What I’m describing here are essentially some of the processes during construction.

Actually, this will be covered in the final lecture. Another point is that we need to review the progress claim, which you’ve already mentioned earlier, and that has also been discussed.

These topics have already been covered. As for the specific tasks to be carried out during the construction phase, we will dedicate a later session to explain them in detail. At that time, I will share some documents with you, such as the documents that need to be issued from the design institute’s perspective, and may also discuss what shop drawings submitted by contractors to the design institute look like.

During the technical feasibility study, technical data is requested from suppliers or manufacturers to assess equipment viability. This requires ongoing communication to obtain technical specifications, datasheets, and other relevant materials.

A key consideration is lead time, or supply cycle. In North America, lead times for large equipment are typically around one year, and during the pandemic, they were even longer. This directly affects project scheduling.

The lead time for large equipment in North America is typically around one year, and it was even longer during the pandemic, directly impacting project schedules.

During the detail design phase, technical support from suppliers of large or complex equipment is often required. While engineers are experienced, projects involve a wide range of technical issues, and specific operational, performance, or application-related questions still need to be clarified with suppliers to confirm equipment feasibility. Equipment manufacturers sometimes provide technical literature that goes beyond standard technical manuals. For example, manufacturers of generators, fire alarm systems, or building automation systems not only supply products but also conduct technical promotions, such as Lunch & Learn sessions.

Unlike in China, where people might be invited to visit factories or attend recreational events, here, since these are private companies, everything is billed by the hour. A common practice is for manufacturers to introduce their products during Lunch & Learn sessions—where attendees eat lunch while listening to product presentations. These typically last one to one and a half hours. Many major manufacturers, such as Eaton, Siemens, or Square D, also publish White Papers, which contain valuable technical reference materials.

Another term is Startup service during construction—what does this mean?

Generally speaking, larger-scale projects or more important and complex equipment/systems will have a Startup phase. This refers to the period right after the equipment is first activated, where suppliers or manufacturers need to be on-site to ensure proper operation. Contractors should include these costs in their quotes during the bidding stage. Designers can also add a clause in the Specification Book requiring contractors to account for supplier/manufacturer on-site Startup services in their quotes.

Startup services are actually very important, as many complex pieces of equipment require them. That covers coordination with suppliers and manufacturers. Next, let’s discuss how to better coordinate with various Stakeholders.

Startup services are essential because many complex pieces of equipment require them, including coordination with suppliers and manufacturers. Next, let’s discuss how to better coordinate with various stakeholders.

As an engineering designer, no matter how extensive your knowledge, deep your experience, or solid your foundation may be, it is never sufficient. Consulting demands a broad knowledge base and rich experience, requiring continuous skill and expertise development. At the same time, you should also learn the fundamentals of other disciplines, such as architecture or mechanical engineering, to better understand others during coordination and avoid input or alignment conflicts.

Improving personal skills and standards requires constant learning. Fortunately, our field is relatively traditional—there has been little new content to learn over the years, aside from the application of some new technologies, as the fundamental principles and theories have remained largely unchanged.

After completing each project, we conduct a Lesson Learned session to summarize the experiences and lessons gained during the project execution, aiming to avoid similar mistakes in future projects of the same nature. This is actually a great process for improvement.

Additionally, internal checks and reviews among different disciplines within our team are very helpful for learning. Peer review involves inviting professionals from third-party companies in the same field to conduct the review—preferably those at least at your level or higher. If they are more experienced, they can point out your shortcomings or oversights, allowing you to learn and ensuring fewer issues when coordinating with other disciplines or stakeholders.

During the coordination process, communication skills are crucial, and proper documentation—including file categorization and management—is essential. This is also a key component of effective communication.

Furthermore, familiarity with local knowledge or requirements from regulatory authorities, such as local power utility regulations, is necessary.

Or some requirements from the telecommunications company. Additionally, for example, a project may have an execution plan, a protocol, or a standardized process, which is also very important. Furthermore, during project execution, when coordinating with other disciplines or stakeholders, if there are any changes, they must be fully and accurately documented for record-keeping, which is also a very good practice. That’s what I’ll talk about.

Coordination between different disciplines is actually extremely important, and such coordination could be cross-border, involving numerous specialties. For example, in one project I worked on, there were program architects (specialized architects responsible for theater design) as well as architects who produced construction drawings. From our perspective, program architects handled conceptual designs, while others focused on construction documentation. Additionally, there were teams responsible for MEP (mechanical, electrical, and plumbing) and municipal engineering.
This is a great example of effective communication. At the time, I was working for a very large Canadian oil pipeline company, representing the client as the Electrical Project Lead.

This is a great example of effective communication. At the time, I was working for a very large Canadian oil pipeline company, representing the client as the Electrical Project Lead.

The project was actually an oil pipeline project with a budget of approximately 50 to 100 million dollars. The company did an excellent job during the design phase: they allocated sufficient time and design fees, so everything was thoroughly considered, and all details were well addressed. By the construction phase, there were very few change orders, roughly less than five percent.

The project progressed quickly with minimal change orders. Every stakeholder involved was highly experienced, from design to construction to management. As a result, the project advanced very smoothly, and coordination was seamless.

This is the best project I’ve worked on in North America over the years: within budget, on time, and with excellent quality. This is the second example, showcasing good coordination.

Let me talk about examples of poor coordination. This was an industrial project in Vancouver – the Zhi Jiang Factory. After purchasing the site, the Asian client initiated a renovation project for the factory. Eager for quick results, they tendered the project when the design was only 60–70% complete. The design team wasn’t particularly skilled either, with many unprofessional aspects. After construction began following the tender, various change orders emerged, ultimately exceeding the original contract value and blowing the budget, while significantly delaying the schedule.

The problems stemmed from an inexperienced new design team and poor coordination between different disciplines. Issues existed in both design and construction phases, with poor integration among various contractors. This became a negative case study—the project was eventually completed after significant delays and cost overruns.

Another example involves Asian clients coming to Canada unfamiliar with local processes and regulations, paying high tuition fees. They should have adapted to local practices earlier, but their persistent application of Asian operational methods led to major losses.

When I worked in Alberta’s oil and gas sector, an Italian national oil company entering Canada for a project also incurred substantial costs. That large-scale project (approximately 2–3 billion) only reached the FEED stage; it is unclear whether it continued, but their coordination appeared ineffective.

In a Dalian project, HVAC and structural disciplines failed to coordinate—the HVAC team designed a fresh air intake that the structural team didn’t account for. After construction, they had to cut through 500–600 mm thick reinforced concrete walls, which would be unthinkable abroad as it compromises structural integrity (foreign engineers wouldn’t approve). Surprisingly, the contractor didn’t charge extra for such change orders to either designers or clients—domestic contracts typically use lump-sum pricing covering everything.

No big deal, I’ll just help you get it done—it’s not like I’m short on cash. Yeah, these are all examples of poor coordination. Regarding coordination between the electrical discipline and other disciplines, as well as with other stakeholders, we’ll stop here for now.

Hello Professor, I’d like to ask a non-scientific question: What’s the general situation regarding the use of aluminum alloy cables here in North America?

Aluminum alloy cable?

Yes, are there any standards or practices that determine whether a project can be used or not?

Regarding this one, when you mention aluminum alloy cable, do you mean that the conductor itself is made of aluminum alloy, not copper or pure aluminum? Is that what you’re referring to?

Yes, aluminum core is already a broad concept. For aluminum core and copper core, most students should have no problem understanding. It mainly depends on certain low-voltage cables—typically robust ones—that can accommodate situations where aluminum cores are used.

For your low-voltage and medium-low-voltage systems, the cables are basically either copper or aluminum. For general commercial or industrial applications, copper is typically used; for residential or less critical applications, aluminum is also acceptable. However, using aluminum alloy for medium-low voltage is relatively rare. For high-voltage applications, like steel-reinforced aluminum conductors (ACSR), those do exist. The key issue is that I’ve never seen this type of product in the market. Because cables here must comply with local standards, and I haven’t come across this kind before. Okay.

(Note: “钢芯铝绞线” is technically translated as “steel-reinforced aluminum conductor (ACSR),” a standard term in electrical engineering.)

I’m quite interested too, is this medium and low voltage you’re referring to?

Yes, domestically, 380 volts is generally the standard low-voltage level.

Yes, domestically, 380 volts is generally the standard low-voltage level.

So here’s a question: Is it aluminum core with copper coating, or copper core with aluminum coating? Oh, the conductor is aluminum, or perhaps aluminum alloy.

Oh.

Currently, it is more commonly permitted for residential use domestically, and it can also be used in non-crowded public places, though with greater difficulty. There is a domestic manufacturer that has developed some fire-resistant flexible conductors and is actively promoting them.

At least in North America, there isn’t this kind of direct radiation method. Aluminum wires can be used in North America, and the regulations don’t prohibit the use of aluminum wires. But regarding the aluminum alloy you mentioned, I have two questions: First, does its conductivity improve compared to aluminum?

This is the first point. Second, how does its weight or price compare to aluminum wire? Let’s not compare it to copper wire?

It contains some additional fine-tuning elements, and its conductivity is even better than that of pure aluminum, while its hardness is also superior.

Hmm,

The overall performance is definitely higher than that of aluminum wire, but its cost is actually about 40% lower than that of copper wire.

This hasn’t been seen yet, it should be a relatively new product. But typically in North America, here’s how it works: when a new product comes along, without a trial period or certification from an authorized body, it won’t be listed in the specifications as approved for use.

When a new product comes along without a trial period or certification from an authorized body, it won’t be listed in the specifications as approved for use.

Okay, let me ask another question. As you mentioned, poor coordination on projects is actually quite common domestically. The construction drawings are only, say, X percent complete when the client starts pushing for progress, and then construction begins. This issue is quite prevalent, and there aren’t really any good methods to avoid this cycle of repeated construction and demolition.

This issue is indeed quite severe. For instance, we currently have a project where formal drawings weren’t even finalized in the early stages—construction proceeded floor by floor, only to discover problems after completion, leading to demolition and rework. This problem is really hard to avoid, and in the end, it results in a lot of waste.

Haste makes waste—this is fundamentally a systemic issue across society. Everyone is caught in a rat race, fiercely competing, afraid of falling behind. Many might feel trapped by circumstances, and I believe it’s largely shaped by the broader environment. Additionally, the mechanisms here are different compared to North America. Over there, even minor issues are scrutinized and debated extensively.

The cost of projects in China is five times lower than in North America—at least five times lower. In other words, North American project costs are at least five times higher than China’s, but their timelines and durations are also five times longer. The scale of development China achieved in decades would take over a century to replicate in North America. Things are slow here, forming a stark contrast with China—where competition intensifies and speed keeps increasing, here it’s the opposite, slowing down gradually. People here don’t perceive it as slow; it’s a gradual deceleration, so they don’t notice. Many who were born and live here consider this pace normal.

Having worked in both China and here, I’ve seen the contrast firsthand. Canada is indeed very slow, while the U.S. is faster than Canada. The pace in the U.S. is acceptable—competition is fiercer, relatively more intense, and they tend to maintain better quality control. If they could slightly increase speed while keeping their current operational model, it’d be ideal. China is a bit too caught up in the rat race; focusing more on quality and easing up on the relentless drive might lead to better outcomes.

You see, even back when we were doing design work, as you mentioned, the gap in drawing quality was indeed quite significant. Our drawings here are extremely detailed, but we actually have many big and small issues—almost all of which end up being resolved by the on-site construction teams.

OK, speaking of this, let me talk about the differences between North America and China. In North America, construction crews rely entirely on design institutes and won’t make any decisions on their own. They follow the drawings exactly as they are, down to the simplest line or most basic operation—nothing is done without approval from the design institute. Design fees here are also much higher—in China, it might be around 1-2%, at most 2-3%, whereas in North America, it’s at least 5%, even up to 5-10%. For example, our engineering supervision fees here are 8% to 10% of the project cost.

The workload here is immense: first, the design must be extremely detailed, and second, a lot of effort goes into the construction phase. In my five or six years working in China, once the drawings were issued, there was hardly anything to do—only major issues the contractor couldn’t resolve would come to you. Here in North America, even the smallest issue requires your attention, with endless paperwork to handle. This creates a situation where engineers in North America have more growth opportunities—they need a broad knowledge base and high standards, covering management, technology, coordination, cost control, and on-site construction issues. Because when problems arise, contractors push everything onto the design institute.

In China, at least from my experience, contractors are highly experienced. Whether the design institute’s drawings are good or bad, the contractor will manage to complete the job and only come to you as a last resort. If they can solve it themselves, they will. That’s my impression.

In China, take our television industry design institutes for example—no matter how large the factory is, they only allocate you one or two months. Has the timeline gotten even shorter now?

Thirty days.

Thirty days,  
Yeah, back then it took me almost two months, and now it’s thirty days. You know, some things that used to take a day or two, or a week to finish—here, what you guys do in thirty days would take us over five months. Government projects are even slower. Even small projects take one or two years, which is unbelievable. That’s why I say it’s at least five times more professional—so when they deliver, their projects are very unlikely to have major errors.  
Yes, that’s exactly how we do it. I see that even our own designers are responsible for preparing the cost estimates—the final project cost calculations—we handle that ourselves too, the quantities.  
Are you talking about North America?  
Yes, yes, yes.

In terms of project quantities, the design institute’s estimates during our budgeting process are relatively rough, mainly used for applying for budgets and funds. When it comes to preparing budgets for major projects, they still engage specialized budgeting companies, as we’re not professionals in this field. However, you must have a general understanding here, such as market rates: what price range this equipment falls into, how much workers cost per hour—these are the most fundamental aspects.

For designers or when working on a specific project, like installing a switchboard, you should have a rough idea of how many man-hours are required. Otherwise, how can you prepare a budget? But the accuracy doesn’t need to be extremely high—we can’t achieve that level of precision.

When we need to calculate quantities from drawings, such as the length of cables or pipelines, is it usually done manually? Or is there software for that?

This isn’t something our design institute handles. Most of it falls under the contractor’s responsibility—they figure it out themselves. As you’ve seen from the drawings, we don’t even specify the routing details; they measure it on their own. This actually reduces a significant workload for our design institute—they just estimate it themselves anyway. They’ll take our drawings and make their own assessments. In fact, in this regard, domestic practices differ from international ones. Overseas, they tend to be even more hands-off, pushing this part entirely onto the contractors.

Okay, thank you, Teacher Fan.

It’s okay, let’s see if anyone else has any questions.

It’s okay, let’s see if anyone else has any questions.

Hello, Professor Fan. As contractors, we sometimes need to submit a change order to the design institute as a consultant, which is referred to as a “variation.” How can we streamline the procedural handling to make it faster and more convenient?

Exactly.

Exactly.

OK, when you mentioned "change order," from which perspective are you speaking? Are you the contractor or the design institute? From my perspective as the contractor. Oh, then you need to follow the process—what I call "going through the procedure." You have this change order, and as I just explained the process, there might be more details to discuss later, or perhaps we’ll revisit or delve deeper into it.

This part doesn’t seem workable. That part was overlooked.  
This approach clearly increases my workload—both materials and labor.  
This is additional work. I can do it, but it will cost this much.  
Once approved, it becomes a change order.

For international contractors, no work begins until the change order is approved. Unlike in China, where people might say, “Hey, just do it first—the money won’t be an issue.” Overseas, it’s strict: without an approved change order, I won’t start the work for you.

Actually, it’s faster to follow the process step by step in this part.

Yes, you definitely have to proceed step by step—what else can you do? Asking for money directly isn’t appropriate either. Every step of these procedures must be clarified, documented, and calculated properly.

Let me give you an example: Back when we were building a chip factory in China, it involved a collaboration between two North American companies—one as the main contractor and the other as a subcontractor. In the end, over 3 million RMB went unpaid due to contract disputes and scope disputes. Later, they specifically flew two lawyers from California to handle it, costing over $7,000 USD.

But think about it—those lawyers didn’t understand the situation either. They had to talk to you, gather evidence, go to court, and so on. So if you properly archive all kinds of evidence, whether emails, written correspondence, or anything else, it becomes a huge advantage when dealing with financial or contract disputes in future lawsuits.

Teacher Fan, I have another question: You mentioned earlier that the homeowners’ association has the right to review the shop join drawings for the castle. Generally speaking, how much time in advance should we submit the shop join drawings to the homeowners’ association for review during construction?

Not only as fast as possible.

Not only as fast as possible,  
That’s right,  
The design package already includes specifications with shop drawing submission requirements for each type of equipment in the specification. Once you receive this, as a contractor, after signing the contract with the owner, you should immediately use these technical drawings to prepare shop drawings, as this is your first step. After preparing the shop drawings, submit them to the design institute, and only after the design institute approves them can you proceed with ordering. Construction can only begin after the equipment and materials arrive on site, so shop drawings are essentially your first checkpoint.  
Then for this shop join drawing, it’s best to submit it together with my order documents, materials, and dimensions—no, after doing it this way,

Then for this shop join drawing, it’s best to submit it together with my order documents, materials, and dimensions—no, after doing it this way.

Your shop drawings are the highly detailed technical documentation for ordering these materials and equipment, including drawings, descriptions, and technical specifications, right? Once the construction contract is signed, you’ll follow the design institute’s instructions to determine which equipment and materials are needed and the required submission depth. Then you immediately contact the manufacturer or supplier, send them the design institute’s specifications directly, and say this is the submittal required by the design institute—prepare it quickly for me.

What mainly affects whether we accept the drawings are some dimensions and technical parameters. As contractors, we request these to confirm whether the critical parts affecting us are feasible. Is this approach viable?

What exactly are you referring to when you say “get the dimensions from whom”? Do you mean technical specifications?

With the manufacturer.

What exactly are you referring to when you say “get the dimensions from whom”? Do you mean technical specifications?

With the manufacturer.

Here’s the thing: as a foreign design institute, if they want to review the drawings, they expect the complete set. It’s not like they’ll accept a preliminary design document first, review it once, then wait for a full set to review again—that’s not how it works.

He wants the manufacturer’s parameters, and it should be a complete set of parameters.

He wants the manufacturer’s parameters, and it should be a complete set of parameters.

I’m just reviewing your complete submission. If you provide an incomplete one, I’ll send it back and point out what’s missing, then you’ll need to resubmit. Thank you, Professor Fan. Everyone clear on that? Yes, hello Professor Fan, I’d like to ask about MEP fields. As you just mentioned, the domestic competition is extremely intense now. What we’re wondering is: if we want to become international-standard MEP engineers or designers, what would be a well-established development path for us?

Since you’re a perfect example of transitioning from domestic to international markets, could you share some relevant experience? Specifically, what competencies do we need to participate in the international design market, or to become a qualified MEP engineer for international projects? You’ve raised two questions, yes, two questions.

For you personally, to become an engineer in North America (USA, Canada), you’ll likely need at least four years of work experience and a bachelor’s degree. If you have an overseas degree, the engineering association here will have an evaluation committee assess your educational background. If they recognize your domestic qualifications, that hurdle is cleared; if not, you may need to submit transcripts or take supplementary exams.

Regarding work experience, you need at least four years, with one year being local experience. This means your domestic experience might count for three years, and you’ll still need one year of local experience. In other words, you must work for a company here under the supervision of a Professional Engineer to complete that year.

To become licensed, you must pass a professional exam covering engineering law and professional ethics—this is not a technical test. After passing, you can apply for your engineering license.

If your overseas degree is not recognized, you may need to complete additional technical or specialized courses, as determined by the engineering association.

For companies, registration is required to undertake engineering consulting or design projects, and they must have licensed engineers on staff. You can apply to join a locally qualified design firm. Starting a consulting company or obtaining local qualifications is relatively straightforward. However, for large-scale projects such as construction or design, a local company’s official stamp and signature are typically required, as unqualified firms lack the necessary authority.

Not to mention language (there’s English too, so I won’t dwell on that), I’ll focus on the differences in responsibilities between engineers here and those back in China. I worked in China for several years, where the job basically involved drawing blueprints—sometimes going to the site, sometimes not. Your lead engineer or senior engineer would tell you how to draw, and you’d follow their instructions. There was little cross-disciplinary communication with the design institute; your role ended after the design phase.

For example, tasks like budgeting or understanding the entire project lifecycle—I had no clue about bidding processes because we weren’t involved at all, right? During construction, they’d only reach out if problems arose. There was no construction management or reviewing discrepancies—nothing. Once the project was completed, inspections and handovers had nothing to do with us. Back in China, your job was pretty much done after finishing the drawings.

Here, it’s completely different. For government or large-scale projects here, the design fee breakdown is roughly 60–65% for design work, 5% for bidding support, and 35% for construction-phase services. In other words, if the design fee is $10,000, $3,500 is allocated to services during construction.

To coordinate confidently, you must constantly broaden your expertise across disciplines. You need to understand the entire project workflow, including budgeting, labor hours, and rough material costs, as well as the bidding and construction processes.

From a technical design perspective, you must master codes and design principles while also understanding on-site issues, including system-to-equipment specifics from manufacturers. Engineers here wield far greater authority than in China. Back home, clients or authorities could demand changes on a whim, even during construction, without notifying you. Here, that is not possible— as the stamped engineer, I have the final say on technical electrical matters. No one can make changes without my signed approval.

Here, your technical authority is immense, but so are the risks and responsibilities you shoulder. You’re accountable for everything—if something goes wrong, it’s on you. To handle such responsibility and risk, you’d better be rock-solid. Can you afford to be mediocre?

During site meetings or client discussions, you must have answers to every question. Even if you don’t, you need enough industry knowledge to earn respect. If you’re well-versed across the board, workers and contractors will respect you.

Here, engineers truly focus on technology, especially at the senior or principal level—many transition into project management. You’re managing projects within your discipline, overseeing technical or procedural aspects for clients, which demands high competence.

I’ve met many Chinese immigrants here who refuse to get their engineering licenses. Why?

Many Chinese immigrants here refuse to get their engineering licenses. He was afraid that after taking on the task, the boss would ask him to revise and amend the documents. He lacked confidence and felt immense pressure. In China, senior or chief engineers with more experience, having seen and handled diverse situations, can cope better. However, younger engineers have relatively fewer opportunities for on-site training, so their exposure is more limited. In contrast, abroad, some freshly graduated engineers are directly sent out to troubleshoot issues. For example, they might be told, “Xiao Zhang, there are some problems with this project—go to the site and handle it.” This reflects comprehensive competency. In China, the process mostly ends after design completion, with little opportunity for on-site practice.
